946.hook: the Jews of Spain are expelled; tradition says the last left near Tisha B'Av
946.howItsDone: Sephardic Jews remember the expulsion from Spain in history, song and family stories, and on Tisha B'Av Jews fast and read the book of Lamentations while sitting low.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conversos, and a lamp burning in a jar. Your line was hidden faith. Did you give someone's quiet custom room? Today, a new week, and the choice put to the Jews of Spain who had never been baptized. Day nine hundred forty-six.

A large iron key hangs on a nail in a kitchen far from Spain. It opens nothing in this house. It belonged to a door in Toledo, or Seville, or a small town in Aragon, and the family that carried it away kept it, and their children kept it after them. Tradition says some Sephardic families held on to keys like this for generations, as if one day they might go home and turn the lock. Today, the year that key was carried out.
screen: `AN IRON KEY ON A NAIL.` → `A DOOR IN SPAIN.` → `KEPT FOR GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: In 1492 the king and queen of Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella, signed an edict of expulsion. Its own words give the reason: Jews living among the conversos, it said, were drawing them back to Judaism. So every Jew who would not be baptized had to leave the kingdoms, by a deadline only a few months away. They could sell their property and take their goods, but not gold, silver or coin. A chronicler of the time wrote of houses sold for almost nothing and vineyards traded for cloth. Some families chose baptism and stayed, and joined the conversos we met yesterday. Others packed and went: to Portugal, to North Africa, to Italy, to the lands of the Ottoman sultan. Tradition says the last of them left Spain around Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of both Temples in Jerusalem. On that day Jews sit low and read the book of Lamentations, which opens with a city sitting alone that was once full of people. For the exiles of Spain, that old lament now had a new city in it. The exiles called themselves Sephardim, after Sepharad, a place named by the prophet Obadiah that Jewish tradition came to read as Spain. They carried Spain with them: its language, which became Ladino, its songs, its recipes, its ways of chanting prayer. Expelled from Sepharad, they kept being Sephardim wherever they landed. The key on the nail is one way to remember. The name is another.
screen: `THE EDICT OF EXPULSION.` · `BAPTISM OR DEPARTURE.` · `AROUND TISHA B'AV.` · then, large: `SEPHARDIM WHEREVER THEY LANDED.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of a home that was lost. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a home you can't go back to: a childhood house, a grandparent's apartment, a town your family left, or a home someone you love had to leave. Find one sound from it, one smell, one view from a window. Name them quietly, one at a time. Let them stay with you for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Sephardim. The name Spain's exiled Jews took for themselves, after Sepharad, carrying Spain's language, songs and prayers wherever they landed. Today's word.
Your line: the key on the nail. Today, find one object in your home that came from somewhere else, and learn or tell its story. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Don Isaac Abravanel
947.hook: a royal minister who chose exile with his people
947.howItsDone: Abravanel's Bible commentaries are still studied, and his own account of the expulsion is read by those who study the Spanish exile; some Jews remember the expulsion on Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1492: the order that ended open Jewish life in Spain, and your line, the key on the nail. Whose lost home did you hold in mind? Today, one man who could have stayed behind, and didn't. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

A man stands in a royal palace with a purse he hopes will change a king's mind. He has served the crown of Castile with money and with figures. He knows the rulers by sight; they know him by name. The order to expel the Jews has been signed, and he has come to plead. Tradition says he offered a great sum, and that for a moment it seemed to work. Then the door closed. Some tellings say he could have kept his place at court, if he would be baptized. Today, Don Isaac Abravanel.
screen: `A PURSE AND A PLEA.` → `THE DOOR CLOSES.` → `A PLACE AT COURT, FOR A PRICE.`

segments.voice: Don is a Spanish title of honor. Isaac Abravanel was a financier who had served rulers in Portugal and then in Spain, and he was also a scholar who wrote long commentaries on the books of the Bible. That double life matters for his story. In the preface to his commentary on the book of Kings, he tells it in his own words: how he went before the king again and again, how he begged, how friends at court pleaded too, and how none of it moved the decree. Another court Jew he had worked beside, Abraham Seneor, accepted baptism and stayed. Abravanel did not. He left Spain with the rest of the exiles, carrying his books, and spent his last years moving from city to city, Naples, Corfu, Monopoli and at last Venice, still writing. His commentaries are still read and printed today, and they open with long lists of questions before he answers any of them. The book of Ruth has a line that fits the shape of what he did. Ruth, a widow from Moab, is told she may go back to her own home. She answers her mother-in-law: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Ruth chose a people she was not born into. Abravanel chose the people he was born into, at the moment it cost him everything the court could give. Notice what he did not do. He did not save the community; he failed at that. What he did was refuse to be saved apart from them. His name stayed with the exiles because he went where they went.
screen: `A MINISTER AND A SCHOLAR.` · `HE PLEADED WITH THE KING.` · `A COLLEAGUE STAYED. HE DID NOT.` · then, large: `WHITHER THOU GOEST.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: stand with your people. Sit tall, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Bring to mind the people you belong to: a family, a congregation, a neighborhood, a crew at work. Picture them leaving a place together, walking a road. Now see yourself in that line, not watching from a window. Notice what it feels like in your body to be counted with them. If you pray, you can say Ruth's words quietly: thy people shall be my people. Stay in that line while the bell holds the time.
Abravanel. A minister of kings and a Bible commentator who pleaded against the 1492 expulsion, failed, and chose exile with the people he could not save. Today's word.
Your line: he left with them. Today, when someone in your circle is having a hard time, find one small way to stand next to them instead of watching. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

948.title: Portugal, 1497
948.hook: Portuguese Jews are forcibly converted en masse
948.howItsDone: Jews remember the forced conversions in Spain and Portugal in history and story, and some descendants of New Christian families today study their roots and return to Jewish life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Don Isaac Abravanel, the minister who refused to be saved alone. Your line was he left with them. Whose side did you stand at? Today, the road west, to the next border. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

For exiles in western Spain, the nearest way out was not the sea. It was Portugal, just next door. Families who had left Spain crossed into it with what they could carry, and for a short while it looked like a refuge. They had paid to enter. They spoke a language close to their own. Then a new king of Portugal arranged a royal marriage with the house of Spain, and the terms of that marriage reached the refugees. The door they had walked through was about to become a trap. Today, Portugal.
screen: `THE BORDER NEXT DOOR.` → `A SHORT REFUGE.` → `A ROYAL MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: King Manuel ordered the Jews of Portugal to leave. Then he made it almost impossible for them to go. Chroniclers of the time, Jewish and Christian, tell what followed. Children were taken from their parents to be baptized and raised as Christians. Adults gathered at the port of Lisbon, waiting for the promised ships, were baptized by force instead. Spain had at least offered a choice between baptism and exile. Here the exit was closed and the choice was made for them. A Jewish writer of the next generation, Samuel Usque, wrote a book of consolation for these families, and he tells of parents who grieved for children carried away. The people who came out of this were called New Christians. Some of them became Christians in heart over time. Others kept what they could of Judaism in secret, and in Portugal some kept it a very long time. In the twentieth century an engineer named Samuel Schwarz, working in the hills of the north, met families who still said their own prayers by heart, in Portuguese, and he wrote those prayers down. We met the Hebrew word for people baptized against their will a few days ago: anusim, the forced ones. Jewish law holds that a person acting under force is not to blame, and rabbis applied that to the anusim, though they argued over those who later could have left and stayed. There is a psalm that speaks for people who suffer and still hold on. Psalm forty-four: "All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten Thee." That line describes what the hidden families tried to do. They could not live as Jews in the open. They tried not to forget. And their grandchildren and great-grandchildren would turn up later in this story, in other ports, asking to come home to a Judaism their families had carried in secret.
screen: `AN ORDER TO LEAVE, AND NO WAY OUT.` · `BAPTIZED BY FORCE.` · `NEW CHRISTIANS, SOME IN SECRET.` · then, large: `YET HAVE WE NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember those who were forced. Let your hands rest open on your lap. Bring to mind a parent at a harbor, waiting for a ship that never came. Hold that one picture. Then widen it to anyone you know of who was made to give up something they loved: a language, a name, a faith, a home. You don't need to fix anything. Remembering is the whole practice. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: yet have we not forgotten Thee. The bell holds the time.
Portugal. The refuge next door that closed: Jews ordered out, kept from leaving, and baptized by force, some of whom kept their Judaism in secret. Today's word.
Your line: they tried not to forget. Today, say one line you know by heart, a prayer, a song, a saying, and remember the families who kept theirs by memory alone. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: Welcomed in
949.hook: the Ottoman sultan takes in refugees in Salonika and Istanbul
949.howItsDone: Sephardic communities still keep customs, melodies and songs in Ladino that trace back to the exiles who settled in Ottoman lands, and Jewish law and teaching stress welcoming the stranger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Portugal: a refuge that closed, and families baptized by force. Your line was they tried not to forget. Did a small lamp or a set table bring them to mind? Today, a door that opened. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

Ships come into a crowded harbor at the far end of the Mediterranean. On board are families who have lost one home, and some of them a second. They carry Spanish on their tongues, a few books, the names of streets they will never walk again. The question on every deck is the same: will anyone let us off this boat? In the lands of the Ottoman sultan, the answer was yes. Today, welcomed in.
screen: `SHIPS IN A CROWDED HARBOR.` → `STREETS THEY WILL NOT SEE AGAIN.` → `WILL ANYONE LET US IN?`

segments.voice: The Ottoman sultan Bayezid the Second allowed the exiles from Spain to settle in his lands. They came to Istanbul, to Salonika, today's Thessaloniki in Greece, and to other port towns. Tradition tells a story about him: that he said the king of Spain had made his own country poorer and the sultan's richer. Nobody can be sure he said it, but the story says something people believed. The newcomers brought trades, printing presses, medicine and learning. What they found was not equality. Jews lived under the rules for non-Muslims, paid a special tax, and depended on the ruler's good will. But they could pray openly, keep their own courts and schools, and raise children as Jews. After Spain and Portugal, that was a great deal. Look at what they built. In Salonika, congregations formed by home town, each keeping the customs of the city it came from, with names like Lisbon, Aragon and Catalonia. Their Spanish became a Jewish language of its own, written in Hebrew letters, which we now call Ladino or Judeo-Spanish. The Torah gives the reason for welcome in plain words. In Exodus: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." That verse speaks to Israel about strangers in its own land. Here the roles were turned: the exiles were the strangers, and another people opened the gate. Being welcomed in did not erase what was lost. It made it possible to keep the rest.
screen: `THE SULTAN OPENS HIS LANDS.` · `NOT EQUAL, BUT FREE TO PRAY.` · `CONGREGATIONS NAMED FOR HOME.` · then, large: `YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome one refugee or newcomer. Settle your breath. Remember your own first week somewhere new: a school, a job, a city. What did you not know yet that someone could have told you? Where the bus stops, which shop is open late, who to ask. Now bring to mind a person who is in that first week right now, perhaps someone who arrived from far away. Choose one practical thing you could hand them, and hold it in mind while the bell holds the time.
Welcomed in. The exiles from Spain settling in Ottoman lands, in Istanbul and Salonika, free to live openly as Jews and to keep the customs of their home towns. Today's word.
Your line: another people opened the gate. Today, do the one small welcoming thing you chose, for one person who is new. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Doña Gracia Nasi
950.hook: a converso businesswoman who organized escapes for many
950.howItsDone: Doña Gracia Nasi is remembered in Jewish communities as a rescuer and patron, and her story is often told alongside Esther's as a woman who used her position for her people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, welcomed in: exiles settling in Istanbul and Salonika, congregations named for home. Your line was another people opened the gate. Who did you let in? Today, a woman who helped people get to those doors. Day nine hundred fifty.

A merchant's letter goes out from a counting house in Antwerp. On paper, it is about pepper, cloth and credit. Underneath, it is about people: which family is ready to leave, which road over the Alps is safe this month, which agent in which city will hide them for a night and give them money for the next stage. The woman behind those letters was baptized, rich and watched. She was also running an escape route. Today, Doña Gracia Nasi.
screen: `A LETTER ABOUT PEPPER.` → `REALLY ABOUT PEOPLE.` → `A HIDDEN ESCAPE ROUTE.`

segments.voice: She was born into a family of New Christians in Portugal, the families we met two days ago, and she was raised with a Christian name, Beatriz de Luna. She married into a great trading house, the Mendes family, and after her husband and then his brother died, she ran the business herself. Her firm dealt in spices and banking across Europe. That network of ships, agents and credit became something else in her hands: a way out. Through her agents, New Christians from Portugal could travel north to Antwerp, then over the mountains into Italy, and on toward the Ottoman lands where they could live openly as Jews. She moved that way herself, through Antwerp, Venice and Ferrara, sometimes under arrest, sometimes in court battles over her fortune. Along the way she took up a Jewish name, Gracia Nasi, and in the end she reached Istanbul, where she lived openly as a Jew. People called her la Señora, the lady. Writers and scholars she supported praised her. Samuel Usque, whose book of consolation we met with Portugal, dedicated it to her. One Jewish story that resembles hers is Esther's: a woman at court hiding who she was, who is told that her place may be the very reason she is there. Mordecai says to her: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" Gracia Nasi did not have a crown. She had ledgers, ships and agents. She used them the way Esther used the palace: for her people.
screen: `BORN A NEW CHRISTIAN.` · `A WIDOW RUNS THE FIRM.` · `TRADE ROUTES BECOME ESCAPE ROUTES.` · then, large: `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: use what you have to rescue. Sit comfortably and take a slow breath. Gracia Nasi didn't invent a new tool; she turned the one in her hands. Look at your own. A phone full of contacts. A car. A spare room. A skill, a language, a few hours a week. Pick one, and ask quietly who it could help get somewhere safer, steadier or less alone. You don't have to act on it in this minute. Just let one answer arrive. The bell holds the time.
Gracia Nasi. A businesswoman born into a New Christian family, who turned a trading network into an escape route and lived openly as a Jew. Today's word.
Your line: la señora. Today, use the one thing you already have, the contact, the car, the skill, to help one person a little further on their way. Day nine hundred fifty.

951.title: Safed
951.hook: a hill town in Galilee becomes the center of Jewish mysticism
951.howItsDone: Tzfat is still a center of Jewish learning and Kabbalah study, and visitors pray in its old synagogues and go up to Meron nearby.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Doña Gracia Nasi, la señora, who turned a trading network into a way out. Your line was la señora. What did you use to help someone along? Today, one of the places the road led. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

A small town clings to a hilltop in the Galilee, in the north of the land of Israel. Stone houses, narrow lanes, a view down to the Sea of Galilee on a clear day. It is not a capital. It has no royal court. And yet, in the generations after the expulsion from Spain, scholars, poets and mystics walked up its slopes and stayed. Some had fled Spain or Portugal; some came from the Ottoman cities we visited; some were born nearby. For a while this hill town was the place to be if you wanted to learn the hidden side of the Torah. Today, Tzfat.
screen: `A TOWN ON A GALILEE HILL.` → `NO CAPITAL, NO COURT.` → `SCHOLARS WALK UP AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Tzfat is the Hebrew name; in English it is often written Safed. Why there? Part of the answer is a mountain nearby, Meron, where tradition places the grave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the sage whom tradition names as the teacher behind the Zohar, a book at the heart of Kabbalah. To live near Meron was to live near the source, as the mystics saw it. Part of the answer is the land itself. For Jews who had lost Spain, there was a pull in living in the land itself, where commandments tied to the soil could be kept and the ancient graves were close. And part of the answer is the people who gathered. In a short span, Tzfat drew a legal scholar who would write a code of Jewish law, a poet who would write a song still sung on Friday night, and a quiet teacher who would change how Jews think about creation and repair. We will meet them over the next days. Running through that circle was a conviction that the exile was not only a disaster in the world, but a crack in something deeper, and that prayer, study and the commandments done with care could help heal it. Psalm 121 is headed a Song of Ascents, which tradition links to pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Its first line fits a hill town too: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" After Spain, some lifted their eyes to that hill and went to find out. Today Tzfat is still a town of synagogues, artists and students.
screen: `TZFAT, OR SAFED.` · `NEAR MERON AND ITS TRADITIONS.` · `A CIRCLE OF SCHOLARS GATHERS.` · then, large: `I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: picture a hill town at dawn. Close your eyes if you like. See stone walls going from gray to gold as the light reaches them. Somewhere a few voices are already singing, low, on the way to prayer. Below, a lake catches the first sun. Let your breath slow to the pace of that waking town. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains. The bell holds the time.
Tzfat. A hill town in the Galilee, near Meron, where scholars and mystics gathered after the expulsion from Spain. Today's word.
Your line: the mystic town. Today, look up at least once, at a hill, a roofline, a patch of sky, and let it be your Tzfat for one breath. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

952.title: The set table
952.hook: Joseph Karo's code of Jewish law, printed in 1565
952.howItsDone: Observant Jews look to the Shulchan Aruch and its commentaries for practical Jewish law, and rabbis still cite it when they answer questions about daily practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tzfat, the hill town in the Galilee. Your line was the mystic town. Where did you look up? Today, the end of the week, and a book that came down from that hill. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Before guests arrive, someone sets the table. The plates go down, the cups, the bread, the salt. Nobody has to hunt in the cupboard. Everything is where your hand expects it. Now, a scholar in Tzfat has spent years on a huge work of Jewish law, tracing every rule back through the Talmud and the great teachers, argument by argument. Then he does something different. He writes a short version, plain and in order, so that a person can find what to do without wading through the debate. He gives it a homely name. Today, Shulchan Aruch.
screen: `BEFORE THE GUESTS ARRIVE.` → `YEARS OF DEEP RESEARCH.` → `THEN, A SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: Shulchan Aruch means a set table. Its author, Rabbi Joseph Karo, first wrote a long commentary called Beit Yosef, the House of Joseph, which gathers the sources and opinions for each law. The Shulchan Aruch is the digest of that work: the rulings without the long trail behind them. In his introduction, Karo explains the name. He wanted the laws laid out like a table already set, so that anyone could sit down and eat. Open it and you find the whole of daily life. How to wake and pray. Shabbat and the festivals. Kosher food, mourning, charity. Marriage and divorce. Business, loans and the courts. Printing let it travel far beyond Tzfat, and rabbis and students in distant cities worked from it, and argued with it. The name has a quiet echo in the Psalms: "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies." For a people still living with the loss of Spain and Portugal, a set table was a strong image: order after chaos, a home that could be carried in a book. And this has been a week of homes lost and found. Spain's decree in 1492. Abravanel, who left with them. Portugal, where the exit closed. The Ottoman lands, where exiles were welcomed in. Gracia Nasi, la señora, who opened escape routes. Tzfat, the mystic town. And now, from that town, a table set for anyone who wants to live by Jewish law, wherever they have landed.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: set your table with care. If you're near a table, or the next time you eat, lay one place slowly: a plate, a cup, a fork, a napkin, each where a hand will reach for it. If you're not near one, do it in your mind. Notice how putting things in order changes the room a little, and you a little. A set table says someone expected you. Breathe with that while the bell holds the time.
Shulchan Aruch. The set table: Joseph Karo's plain, ordered digest of Jewish law, written in Tzfat, laying out daily life so anyone could find their place. Today's word.
Your line: where your hand expects it. Today, set one table on purpose, for yourself or for someone else, and notice what it feels like to sit down to it. Day nine hundred fifty-two.
